newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council considers bans against Angola's UNITA.
newsitem.headline: UN Council considers bans against Angola's UNITA.

text.p: Security Council members on Tuesday threatened to impose unspecificed sanctions against Angola's opposition UNITA movement unless it took concrete steps by Friday to abide by peace agreements.
"We will consider and we will impose appropriate additional measures," said Council President Sir John Weston after private consultations in the 15-member body.
"Let no one say later that they were not warned," he said. "The situation is totally unacceptable"

UNITA has rebuffed bids to integrate territories it controls with those of the government, demobiize its fighters and take other measures necessary to complete the peace process under 1994 agreements signed in the Zambian capital of Lusaka.
Council diplomats said the sanctions, to be considered next week, would depend on a Friday report from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.

They would probably include a travel ban for UNITA officials, including its leader Jonas Savimbi. But they said measures such as freezing UNITA's bank accounts abroad might be too difficult to carry out. The council has imposed an arms embargo against UNITA that has had little impact.

In Lisbon on Tuesday, the Portuguese news agency Lusa, said Savimbi told Thomas Pickering, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for political affairs, as well as U.N. officials in Luanda, that UNITA was ready to hand over territory under control by the end of November. But there was no word on how serious officials considered the overtures.

Unless Annan's report stated that UNITA had "taken irreversible and concrete steps to fulfil its obligations" the council was ready "to consider and to impose appropriate and additional measures," Weston told reporters.

Weston, who is Britain's U.N. ambassador, said, council members believed there could be no peace until UNITA met its obligations, adding: "the international community will not tolerate the resumption of hostilities in Angola."

After two decades of civil war UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, entered into a unity government in April with the ruling MPLA, the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola.
But UNITA still controls large areas of the country, and only a minority of its fighters have been demobilized and incorporated into a new national army.

Fears are growing that the peace process has been unravelling since the civil war in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo, whose former ruler Mobutu Sese Seke had provided assistance in UNITA's campaign.
In May and in June the government launched an offensive into UNITA zones in the northeast, in what military officials in Luanda said was the biggest such operation since 1994.

Consequently UNITA has not abided by U.N. demands to continue demilitarizing its soldiers. And UNITA's reluctance has in turn prompted the government to heighten its preparedness for a possible conflict with the former rebels, diplomats and military officials in Luanda said.
